title: AI flags Julie Knichel's brain hemorrhage before aneurysm treatment and her return to nursing
summary: Julie Knichel’s surgeon said that he used Viz.ai in a case that appears to be hers.
account: Julie Knichel, a 57-year-old nurse, suffered a ruptured brain aneurysm. At Baptist Health's Marcus Neuroscience Institute, AI reviewed her scan and alerted clinicians to the bleeding. They sealed the aneurysm with coils delivered through a catheter. After about three weeks in hospital, she recovered and returned to full-time nursing. Her symptoms began on 2 February 2024. Baptist Health gives the day and month, and Jan Engoren’s subsequent interviews with Knichel and Snelling establish the year. The Viz.ai attribution is inferred from Snelling’s follow-up interview: he names Viz.ai, then describes an ICU nurse with a subarachnoid hemorrhage and points to the hospital’s earlier public account. The clinician, hospital, patient’s occupation, condition, and alert sequence match Knichel’s story. He does not name the nurse in that interview or identify a software module or version.
purpose: Detect brain hemorrhage and alert clinicians.
system: Viz.ai stroke detection and care coordination

ratings.reason: Knichel survived a life-threatening hemorrhage and resumed her work and activities.

ai_role.statement: Viz.ai flagged the bleeding and notified the stroke team. Clinicians treated the aneurysm. The platform attribution follows from the treating surgeon’s subsequent interview and matching published case. Its separate effect on survival was not measured.

evidence.title: Stroke Nurse Shares Her Experience After Brain Aneurysm
evidence.quote: Ms. Knichel is happy to have returned to work full time and to her previous activities
